text: A smart contract is a small, deliberately narrow piece of a decentralized application. Solidity — a separate course in this path — is what you use to write that contract. But a contract sitting on-chain by itself is useless to a normal user; nobody calls it by hand from a command line. Everything a user actually touches, and everything a developer uses to build, test, and operate around that contract, is written in JavaScript or its typed sibling, TypeScript. That's not an accident — JavaScript already runs natively in every browser and, through Node.js, on every server and command-line tool.

JavaScript shows up in three places in every real dApp — short for decentralized application, a frontend plus one or more smart contracts it talks to. The frontend — the actual page with the Connect Wallet button, almost always built in React or Next.js. The libraries that talk to the chain — ethers.js and viem, the two dominant ways to read blockchain data and send transactions. And backend scripts — Node.js code, a JavaScript runtime that runs outside the browser, used to deploy contracts, index on-chain events into a database, or run an automated bot.

It's tempting to skip straight to connecting a wallet and calling a contract, but that code is just JavaScript syntax wrapped around a library call. Here's the roadmap instead. Chapters one and two build JavaScript fluency — fundamentals, then modern ES6-plus syntax, with no blockchain context competing for your attention. Chapter three covers asynchronous JavaScript, critical since every blockchain call is a network request. Chapters four and five bring in TypeScript, then apply it directly to blockchain data and libraries. Chapter six is Node.js basics. Chapter seven is a capstone — a typed script that reads real blockchain data.

You're ready for lesson two once you can name those three places JavaScript shows up in a dApp, and explain in one sentence why a Solidity-only developer still can't ship a usable product — they can write the contract, but not the site, the deploy script, or the tests that prove it works. Next: setting up the dev environment you'll use for the rest of this course.
